zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical aid consulted after independent scan reading: Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, CC BY 4.0. The scan, not the index, governs this transcription. Data: https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html ; license: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ .

runs.text: Limos, & eruas que estão no fun-

lines.note: Mokuzu denotes weed or plant matter at the bottom of the sea. The preceding page's Mocuz- catchword anticipates this headword; fun- begins Portuguese fundo.
Completes fundo do mar, with printed domar joined, then gives becoming weed on the seabed as an image for drowning. The Japanese kaitei no mokuzu construction agrees with the following gloss.
The idiom means to die drowned at sea. The upright S. marks written usage, separate from the italic Portuguese explanation.

Modashigatai is described here as something difficult to escape. The following continuation elaborates the difficulty of extricating oneself; the historical gloss is not replaced by a modern dictionary sense.

The main text completes the difficulty of extrication. At the far right, the separate parenthesis and dentro complete comerſe por dentro from the following row; they remain on their actual printed line rather than being moved into reading order.
Modae means being distressed or inwardly consumed by anxiety. The phrase comerſe por is completed by displaced dentro on the row above, whose physical position is explicitly represented there.
Modae kogare intensifies the distress. The Portuguese grandemẽ- continues onto the next line; no additional principal form is supplied beyond the printed uru.
Completes grandemente and begins an anguished question about what has happened. The Japanese quotation continues across the next two physical lines without added quotation marks.

runs.text: tenni auogui, chini fuxi modaye cogare-

lines.note: The person looks up to heaven, falls to the ground, and writhes in distress. A visible word gap separates fuxi and modaye; OCR had joined them.

runs.text: Lib. 1. Que he iſto, que farei cõ

lines.note: Completes kogareta and cites Feiq., book 1. The Portuguese begins what is this, what shall I do; the scan has the numeral 1, not OCR i, and the citation label remains roman.

runs.text: os olhos no ceo, & deitando ſe em terra afli-

lines.note: The Portuguese describes eyes raised to heaven and casting oneself upon the ground in grief. Afli- continues into afligindoſe on the next row.
Completes the account of a person overcome by affliction. The existing short-s form in desfazia is retained rather than globally converted to long s.

runs.text: Ida que ſe faz aos Camis, & Fotoques.

lines.note: Mōde is a visit to the kami and Buddhist sacred figures or sites. Camis and Fotoques occur within the Portuguese explanation and retain the type actually printed.
Mōde suru is the verbal expression for making that religious visit. Vt is italic, while the Japanese example is roman.

runs.text: O ir à Tera dos Camis, &

lines.note: The verb mōde is defined as going to the temple of the kami and Buddhist figures. Its zzuru principal form is preserved; Tera and Camis are embedded Japanese terms in the Portuguese gloss.
Fotoques completes the preceding temple-visiting definition. It is the pluralized Japanese religious term within a continuing Portuguese sentence, not an independent headword.
Modoki here means reproving or criticizing. The principal forms are retained exactly rather than expanded into modern Japanese forms.
Modori is the intransitive verb to return or turn back. It contrasts with the transitive Modoxi entry two rows below.
This separate Modori is the noun return. The lack of principal forms and the nominal Portuguese gloss distinguish it from the preceding verb.
Modoshi means returning something or causing a return. The causative wording in the Portuguese distinguishes it from modoru rather than making the two entries redundant.
Mōhatsu means hair, paraphrased as kamige. The final t preserves the checked Sino-Japanese ending; the circumflex differs from the carons in the adjacent entries.
Mōhaya means already or by now. Adu. identifies an adverb, and historical Ia corresponds to Portuguese já without adding an unprinted accent.
Mōgan denotes a blind person or blindness in this terse gloss. The caron over o is retained as printed, not adjusted from later pronunciation.

runs.text: Sebe rala de bambus inteiros enlaça-

lines.note: Mogari is an open fence made from whole bamboo poles interlaced with one another. The Portuguese word enlaçados is divided at the physical row boundary.
Completes the description of interlaced bamboo poles. Mogari wo yū gives making or tying such a fence; the long-u caron and the printed hũs abbreviation are retained.
Make this fence translates the preceding example. It refers specifically to the bamboo structure described above.
This verbal mogari means becoming distressed with some impatience, distinct from the fence noun. The scan corrects OCR Aſtigirſe to Afligirſe and the divided ending to impacien-.
Completes the historical spelling impacientia and gives mogatta hito, a restless or impatient person. The unusual Portuguese comechoſo is retained as printed, not normalized from a modern adjective.
The person readily becomes distressed and troubled. Afflige includes an l after the doubled f in the scan, which the OCR omitted.
Mogasa denotes pox; mogasazzura describes a face marked by it. The following Portuguese adjective completes rosto, while the Japanese zzu spelling remains literal.
Pockmarked completes the face description. Bixigoſo is the historical Portuguese form printed here, not a second Japanese entry.
Mogi is an auger or boring tool shaped like a nail. The scan shows two r letters in Verruma, correcting OCR Veruma; the printed grave accent in prègo is retained.

runs.text: Certa laya de ſeda rala. Vt,

lines.note: A separate mogi denotes a kind of loosely woven silk. The example begins a phrase describing garments made from this fabric.
Completes mogino caguinu, coromo and glosses the result as clothing made from this fabric. The visible caguinu is retained without supplying an expected syllable from a later garment-name.
Mōgin refers to bad or disordered thoughts. The written gi and the abbreviation in penſamẽtos remain unchanged rather than being standardized from a modern reading.
Mogirakashi means crossing, interlocking, or entangling one thing with another. The aita principal form is historical morphology, not a damaged version of a modern shita ending.
Completes one thing with another and gives ashi wo mogirakasu, crossing or interlocking the feet. The example illustrates the physical, rather than figurative, sense.

runs.text: os pees, ou por hum ſobre outro encontrãdos.

lines.note: The Portuguese describes crossing the feet or putting one over the other. Pees and encontrãdos retain the printed historical spelling and abbreviation.
Ito wo mogirakasu gives the corresponding action on threads: obstructing or tangling them. Em- continues into the historical verb emburulhar.
Completes emburulhar os fios, to tangle the threads. The unfamiliar internal vowel is part of the printed form, not silently normalized to modern embrulhar.
Mogire is the intransitive counterpart, for things becoming crossed or entangled. The reflexive Portuguese construction continues below.
Completes one thing becoming tangled with another. Ito ga mogiruru exemplifies a thread becoming entangled, contrasting with the transitive example above.
The Portuguese translates the tangled-thread example, then kokoro mogireta extends the image to a troubled mind or heart. The next row explains that figurative use.
The heart is disturbed or confused. This confirms the figurative mental sense of the preceding Japanese expression without changing its literal romanization.
Mogiri is given as another inflectional form with the same meaning. The printed itta is retained and not expanded into a modern conjugation in the canonical text.
Mōgo means a lie or falsehood. The caron over o belongs to this entry and is not inferred from the marks in neighbouring headwords.
Mogui introduces taking or wrenching something by force. The final i in the stem is visible, correcting OCR Mogu; for- continues as força at the top of column 2.
Completes taking something by force of the hands from column 1. The figurative example then begins with the loss of a good retainer or servant.
Losing that servant is compared to having one's hands and feet torn away. The passive mogareta supports the wrenching-away sense; the Portuguese translation begins Mor-.

runs.text: rendo a alguem hum bom criado he como ſe lhe

lines.note: Completes Morrendo and explains the death of a good servant belonging to someone. The comparison continues below rather than asserting an actual bodily injury.
The loss is like having one's feet and hands cut off. A fresh example then begins uri wo, with initial V representing the printed vowel spelling.

runs.text: Colher o melão q̃ainda não eſtà maduro.

lines.note: Uri wo mogu means plucking a melon; the Portuguese specifies one not yet ripe. The printed q̃ainda remains joined instead of receiving an editorial word space.
Mogihanashi has the same taking-off or wrenching-away sense. The historical aita principal form is preserved without inserting the consonants expected in a modern conjugation.
Mōgyō mōsa denotes doing bad deeds and disorderly acts. The Japanese diacritics and the Portuguese grave in màs are retained as distinct marks.
Completes deſordens, disorderly conduct, followed by the upright written-register label S. This is a continuation of the compound entry above.
Mogitori means taking something away by twisting or force. The Portuguese tor- begins torcendo, whose object and manner are specified below.

runs.text: cendo a mão aquem atem, ou tomar por força.

lines.note: The action twists the hand of the person holding the object, or simply takes it by force. The printed joined aquem and atem are retained.
The example asks how a sword could be wrested away when the hand was trembling. Tachi wo ba is divided across the row boundary with the printed hyphen.
Completes the rhetorical question, how could one wrench it away, and cites Mon. The Portuguese then begins its corresponding description of the trembling hand.

runs.text: a mão, como poderia tirar lhe o montante das

lines.note: Continues the question: with his hand trembling, how could he take the large sword from the other's hands? The printed tirar lhe remains separated without an editorial hyphen.
Hands completes the rhetorical question. The final sign is a question mark, not the spurious accented e in OCR mãosẽ.

runs.text: Erua com que ſe dão botoẽs de fogo.

lines.note: Mogusa is the herb used to apply small burning cauteries, described here as buttons of fire. This explains the historical material and practice without adding therapeutic claims.

runs.text: Brio que hum tem com algum fausto, ou

lines.note: Mō-i denotes an imposing or proud bearing associated with pomp or honours. The internal hyphen separates the vowel sequence and is not a line-end break.
Completes honours and gives mō-i wo furū, making a display of that imposing bearing. The printed caron over u and the divided Portuguese aparato are retained.
Completes aparato and explains showing pride or imposing spirit. This is the translation of the preceding Japanese example.

runs.text: Certa laya de lauores, ou folhagem q̃

lines.note: Moiqua is a kind of decorative work or foliage pattern. The headword's unusual vowel sequence is preserved, while q̃ introduces the continuation about the objects bearing the pattern.
The patterns occur on certain pieces or articles. The source leaves their material unspecified here, so the note does not impose a particular textile or craft.
Mōja is a dead person, paraphrased as shinin. The example repeats Mǒ- across the line boundary; its initial M is damaged but visible, correcting OCR Vǒ-.
Completes mōja wo tomurau, performing funeral rites for the dead. The romanization and the historical Portuguese exequias and pellos remain literal.
Commemorating the dead is the alternative Portuguese explanation of the same Japanese expression. The double m in commemoração is preserved.
Mōzei is a multitude of fierce people, with tazei supplied as a Japanese equivalent. The scan ends feroz with a comma, joining the military comparison on the next line.
A body of fighting men supplies the comparison for the fierce multitude above. This limits the gloss more specifically than a neutral crowd.
Mōzen is paraphrased as becoming improperly stained or affected. The Portuguese uses infection metaphorically, as the following reference to sin or thought shows.
Completes algum and identifies a sin or thought as the contaminating influence. This is moral vocabulary in the historical gloss, not a medical description.

runs.text: Certo liuro da China que trata de couſas

lines.note: Mōji names a Chinese book treating moral subjects. The printed ji is retained without replacing the headword by a modern Japanese title or a conjectural Chinese spelling.
Moral matters completes the description of the Chinese book. The short adjective is a genuine continuation line.
Mojike means something being removed or torn off by twisting. The reflexive Portuguese verbs distinguish this from the active Mojiqi entry below.
Completes algũa and specifies twisting as the means by which the object comes away. The printed abbreviation remains on u.

Mojiki is the active action of pulling or wrenching something off by twisting. The printed ijta principal form is retained, including the descending j, rather than regularized from a modern conjugation.
Completes torcendo and explicitly labels the verb active. This confirms the transitive contrast with Mojiqe.
Mōju means a fierce beast, paraphrased as takeki kedamono. The historical q spelling in qedamono remains unchanged.
Mōjutsu is glossed as sorcery and paraphrased as improper arts or practices. The final t is the printed checked ending; the explanation continues below.

runs.text: ſas marauilhoſas feitas polla arte do demonio.

lines.note: Completes cousas and attributes extraordinary feats to the devil's art in the dictionary author's religious framing. The attribution is preserved as historical source language, not adopted as a factual explanation.
Moma is simply glossed as a large bat. The source does not provide enough diagnostic detail to assign a modern species.
Mōmai denotes ignorance or lack of understanding, illustrated by guchi mōmai. Both occurrences show a circumflex, and the Portuguese definition continues below.
Ignorance completes the paired explanation of guchi mōmai. The unaccented printed spelling is retained.
Momen denotes cotton cloth; Canga is retained as the historical Portuguese textile gloss. The following entry separately names the cotton material itself.
Momenwata is cotton, glossed by Algodão. The internal v begins the wata element and should not be discarded in the diplomatic text.
Momi denotes rice still in its husk. The terse historical gloss Bate is preserved literally, not expanded or confused with the separate rubbing verb below.
The verb momi means rubbing with the hand. Mi- begins mi wo momu on the next line; the principal form ôda has a circumflex in the scan.
Completes mi wo momu and describes rubbing or moving one's own body. The Portuguese hũ continues into a following reflexive expression.
Aſi completes the self-directed action. Ase wo momu is then glossed as a horse sweating; the printed xe corresponds to historical se, not a mistaken x.
Momini môde semuru describes attacking with repeated, concentrated force. The scan's circumflex in môde is retained; the Portuguese intensity phrase continues below.

runs.text: todas as forças. ¶ Item, Furar com ver-

lines.note: Completes fighting with all one's strength, then introduces boring with an auger. Ver- continues as ruma at the top of f0329; the separate bottom ruma is a catchword, not another body row.
